label: 2 Peter 1:1–2
text:
"Servant" (doulos) is placed before "apostle" — bondslave first, the office of apostle resting on the more basic identity of one owned outright, not the reverse.

"Obtained" is lachousin, a verb properly used of receiving something by the casting of lots — faith is pictured as an allotment handed out, not a prize earned or a merit accumulated.

"Like precious" translates isotimon, a rare compound built from isos, "equal," and timē, "value, honor" — the faith of these later, largely Gentile readers is declared of identical worth to the apostles' own, not a lesser, derivative grade of the same thing.

"Righteousness" here names the even-handed fairness by which God allots that equal-value faith without partiality, rather than a purely legal or forensic standing.

"Knowledge" is epignōsei, the intensified form of the ordinary word for knowing — a fuller, more precise, experiential knowing that this letter will keep returning to as its central term.
translation: Simon Peter, a slave and emissary of Jesus Christ, to those who have been allotted a faith equal in value to ours, through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ: may grace and peace be multiplied to you in the full knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.

label: 2 Peter 1:3–4
text:
"Divine power" (theias dynameōs) uses the rarer adjective theios rather than the ordinary word for "God's" — a philosophical, almost technical term for what belongs to deity itself, deliberately bracketed with "divine nature" two verses later.

"Given" is dedōrēmenēs, perfect tense — a gift already, completely granted, standing finished rather than arriving piecemeal.

"Virtue" (aretē) carries pagan philosophical weight as the visible manifestation of excellence or power — here specifically the excellence by which God himself "called us."

"Partakers" is koinōnoi, "sharers, partners" — the identical root Peter's earlier letter used for sharing Christ's sufferings, now applied to something far bolder: sharing, however that is to be understood, in God's own nature.

"Corruption" is phthoras, decay — the same root behind aphthartos, "incorruptible," already central to the first letter — escape from it is tied directly to escape from epithymia, "lust, craving," as if decay and desire were two names for a single disease.
translation: Seeing that his divine power has granted us everything pertaining to life and godliness, through the full knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and excellence, through which he has granted us his precious and greatest promises, so that through these you might become sharers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world because of lust.

label: 2 Peter 1:5–7
text:
"Giving all diligence" translates a compound verb, pareisenenkantes, "to bring in alongside" — human effort is pictured as brought in beside God's already-completed gift of verse 3, supplementing it rather than earning it.

"Add" is epichorēgēsate, borrowed from the Greek theater: a chorēgos was a wealthy patron who personally funded a play's chorus and costumes at his own expense, so the verb means to supply lavishly, extravagantly, out of one's own resources — each virtue is to be funded into the next without stinting.

The seven qualities form a chain in which each is "added to" the one before it rather than replacing it — faith carries virtue, virtue carries knowledge, and so on, an ascending structure that later rhetoric would come to call, borrowing this very image, a "climax."

"Temperance" (enkrateia) is mastery over one's own desires; "patience" (hypomonē) is literally a "remaining under," active endurance rather than passive waiting; "godliness" (eusebeia) names reverence expressed in conduct, not private feeling.
translation: And for this very reason, applying all diligence besides, in your faith supply excellence lavishly; and in your excellence, knowledge; and in your knowledge, self-control; and in your self-control, endurance; and in your endurance, godliness; and in your godliness, brotherly affection; and in your brotherly affection, love.

label: 2 Peter 1:8–9
text:
"Abound" is pleonazonta, present participle — a continuous, ongoing overflow, these qualities pictured as still increasing rather than settled into a fixed measure.

"Barren" translates argous, literally "without work" (a- privative plus ergon), and "unfruitful" is akarpous — the pairing describes a faith that produces neither activity nor result.

"Cannot see afar off" is myōpazōn, a rare word found nowhere else in the New Testament and the direct ancestor of the English "myopia" — a vivid, almost comic image of a man squinting, able to see only what is right in front of his face.

"Forgotten" renders an idiom, lēthēn labōn, literally "having taken forgetfulness" — as if forgetting were something actively seized and held onto, not a passive lapse.
translation: For he to whom these things are not present is blind, being shortsighted, having taken forgetfulness of the cleansing from his former sins. But he to whom these things are present, and are increasing, they make him neither idle nor unfruitful in the full knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.

label: 2 Peter 1:10–11
text:
"Give diligence" repeats the spoud- root of verse 5 — the same deliberate effort applied there to building virtue is now aimed at making one's calling secure.

"Sure" is bebaian, a legal and commercial term for a claim that is valid, guaranteed, unable to be overturned — calling and election are to be rendered, in the believer's own experience, as unchallengeable as a properly executed contract.

"Fall" is ptaisēte, "to stumble, trip" — the negative outcome in view is a fall in the path, not a loss of standing already secured elsewhere.

"Ministered abundantly" translates the identical verb epichorēgēthēsetai already used in verse 5 for lavishly supplying virtue — the same extravagant funding that builds the chain of qualities now furnishes, just as lavishly, the entrance into the kingdom itself.
translation: Therefore, brothers, be the more diligent to make your calling and election secure, for doing these things you will by no means ever stumble. For in this way the entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be lavishly supplied to you.

label: 2 Peter 1:12–15
text:
"Tabernacle" (skēnōmati) is the ordinary word for a tent, a temporary dwelling — applied metaphorically to Peter's own body as a structure he expects soon to strike camp from.

"Put off" is a noun, apothesis, "a laying aside" — the same image as removing a garment, used elsewhere of stripping off the old life's sins.

"Decease" translates exodon, literally "exodus, a way out" — the identical word for Israel's departure from Egypt, here applied to Peter's own coming death as a kind of departure into freedom rather than an ending.

"Endeavour" repeats spoudasō, the same root already used twice in this chapter — Peter's own diligence in writing mirrors exactly the diligence he has just urged on his readers.
translation: Therefore I will always be about to remind you concerning these things, though you know them and have been established in the truth present with you. But I consider it right, as long as I am in this tent, to arouse you by way of reminder, knowing that the laying aside of my tent is soon, even as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. But I will also be diligent that, after my exodus, you may be able, on every occasion, to call these things to mind.

label: 2 Peter 1:16–18
text:
"Cunningly devised fables" translates sesophismenois mythois — sophizō describes something made clever, ingeniously contrived, and mythos is simply "myth, story," giving English "myth" directly — Peter denies, in the strongest available terms, that the apostolic message was a clever fiction.

"Eyewitnesses" is epoptai, a technical term borrowed from the mystery religions for initiates who had reached the highest grade, having personally witnessed the climactic vision at the heart of the rite — Peter takes a word for religious spectacle and insists on its most literal, historical sense: he was there, and saw.

"Majesty" (megaleiotētos) and "excellent glory" (megaloprepous doxēs) both use rare, grandiose vocabulary reserved for the highest splendor — the second phrase functions as a reverent circumlocution, naming the Father's glory without naming the Father directly.

"We heard" ties the entire claim to two witnessing senses at once, seeing and hearing, both located at a specific, nameable place: "the holy mount," the scene of the Transfiguration.
translation: For we did not follow cleverly contrived myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we became eyewitnesses of his majesty. For he received from God the Father honor and glory, when such a voice was borne to him from the majestic glory: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. And this voice, borne from heaven, we ourselves heard, being with him on the holy mountain.

label: 2 Peter 1:19–21
text:
"More sure" is bebaioteron, a comparative built on the same bebaios, "firm, guaranteed," already used of one's calling in verse 10 — Peter ranks the written prophetic word as even more certain than his own extraordinary eyewitness experience on the mountain.

"Day star" is phōsphoros, literally "light-bearer" — the morning star, Venus, the direct root of the English "phosphorus."

"Private interpretation" translates idias epilyseōs — idios, "one's own," and epilysis, "a releasing, an unloosing" — the prophecy did not spring from any prophet privately puzzling out and releasing his own meaning; the source lay elsewhere.

"Moved" is pheromenoi, present passive — literally "being borne along," the standard word for a ship carried by the wind — the prophets are pictured neither as silent instruments nor as independent authors, but as men genuinely propelled, under real sail, by the Spirit's own wind.
translation: And we have the prophetic word made more sure, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a lamp shining in a dismal place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts, knowing this first, that no prophecy of scripture becomes a matter of one's own private unloosing. For prophecy was not ever borne by the will of man, but men spoke from God, being borne along by the Holy Spirit.

label: 2 Peter 2:1–3
text:
"Privily...bring in" translates pareisaxousin, a rare compound stacking para- ("alongside") onto eis- ("into") onto agō ("bring") — the picture is smuggling, false teaching slipped in sideways rather than announced openly.

"Damnable heresies" is haireseis apōleias, "heresies of destruction" — hairesis originally meant simply "a chosen opinion, a school of thought," a neutral term Peter now yokes permanently to ruin.

"Bought" is agorasanta, drawn from agora, "marketplace" — redemption pictured as a purchase, making it all the more striking that these teachers are described as themselves bought by the very Master they deny.

"Feigned words" is plastois logois — plastos, "molded, artificially shaped," the direct ancestor of English "plastic" — speech deliberately fashioned into whatever form will sell.

"Lingereth not" (ouk argei) reuses the same argos root already applied to a barren, "unworking" faith back in 1:8 — here it is judgment itself that refuses to sit idle; "slumbereth not" (ou nystazei) personifies destruction as a figure that flatly will not doze off.
translation: But there also arose false prophets among the people, as also among you there will be false teachers, who will smuggle in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction. And many will follow their sensuality, because of whom the way of truth will be spoken against; and in greed they will exploit you with fabricated words — for whom judgment, from long ago, is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.

label: 2 Peter 2:4–9
text:
"Cast them down to hell" translates tartarōsas, a unique verb built directly on Tartarus, the lowest pit of Greek mythology reserved for the worst offenders — the only place in the New Testament this pagan cosmological term is borrowed, applied here to the confinement of fallen angels.

"Chains of darkness" is seirais zophou, "cords of nether-gloom" — zophos is a poetic word for a thick, murky darkness, distinct from the ordinary word for night.

"Spared not" (ouk epheisato) tolls three times across this passage — the angels, the ancient world, Sodom and Gomorrah — a deliberate rhetorical drumbeat of precedent before Peter's readers ever reach the false teachers themselves.

"Turning...into ashes" is tephrōsas, a rare, vivid verb for reducing something to cinders, the only such use in the New Testament.

"Vexed" is ebasanizen, imperfect tense — a continuous, ongoing torment, describing Lot's inner anguish sustained day after day rather than a single moment of distress.
translation: For if God did not spare angels who sinned, but, casting them into Tartarus, delivered them to chains of nether-gloom, kept for judgment; and did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, the eighth, a herald of righteousness, bringing a flood upon a world of the ungodly; and, reducing to ashes the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, condemned them with a catastrophe, setting an example for those about to be ungodly; and rescued righteous Lot, worn down by the licentious conduct of the lawless — for that righteous man, dwelling among them, day after day was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds seen and heard — then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly out of trial, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment.

label: 2 Peter 2:10–11
text:
"Government" translates kyriotētos, an abstract noun for lordship or dominion in general — the false teachers' contempt reaches beyond any single official to authority itself.

"Presumptuous" is tolmētai, "bold, daring ones," and "selfwilled" is authadeis, "self-pleasing" — both nouns rather than adjectives in the Greek, naming these as settled character-types rather than passing moods.

"Speak evil of dignities" more precisely reads "blaspheme glorious ones" (doxas blasphēmountes) — the object is glorious beings, likely angelic powers, not abstract offices.

Against this, angels who are "greater in power and might" bring no "railing accusation" (blasphēmon krisin) even against the fallen — the same word, blasphēmon, links the two halves of the contrast: what genuine angelic power refrains from, these men indulge in freely, with no power at all.
translation: Especially those going after flesh in the lust of defilement, and despising lordship. Daring, self-willed, they do not tremble at blaspheming glorious ones, whereas angels, though greater in strength and power, do not bring against them a blaspheming judgment before the Lord.

label: 2 Peter 2:12–14
text:
"Natural brute beasts" is physika...aloga zōa, "irrational animals, by their very nature" — creatures that operate wholly on instinct, without the reasoning faculty these men were given but refuse to use.

"Made to be taken and destroyed" (gegennēmena eis halōsin kai phthoran) pictures animals literally bred for the purpose of being caught and killed — the false teachers are described as fulfilling, by their own choices, the very fate such creatures are born into by nature.

"Spots and blemishes" (spiloi kai mōmoi) borrows sacrificial vocabulary for the defects that disqualify an offering, turned here to describe corrupt men fouling the church's shared meals.

"Eyes full of adultery" reads more literally "eyes full of an adulteress" (ophthalmous...moichalidos) — the eyes themselves are pictured as embodying the very woman they cannot stop looking for.

"Cannot cease from sin" translates a single rare compound adjective, akatapaustous, "unable to be stopped" — not merely persistent sinners but ones for whom stopping has become, functionally, impossible.
translation: But these, like irrational animals, born by nature for capture and destruction, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destroying, receiving the wages of unrighteousness — counting reveling in the daytime a pleasure, spots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions while feasting together with you; having eyes full of an adulteress and unable to cease from sin, enticing unstable souls, having a heart trained in greed — accursed children.

label: 2 Peter 2:15–16
text:
"Forsaken" is kataleipontes, present participle — an ongoing, continuing abandonment of the straight path, not a single past decision left behind them.

"Reward of unrighteousness" (misthon adikias) reaches back to Numbers 22, where Balaam is offered payment precisely to curse what God has blessed — greed for hire, not simple confusion, is named as his motive.

"Dumb ass" is hypozygion aphōnon, "a voiceless beast of burden" — the striking irony is grammatical as much as narrative: the normally speechless animal is given "man's voice" (phōnē anthrōpou) to rebuke the professional spokesman for God.
translation: Forsaking the straight way, they have gone astray, having followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved the reward of unrighteousness, but received a rebuke for his own transgression: a voiceless beast of burden, speaking with a man's voice, restrained the madness of the prophet.

label: 2 Peter 2:17–19
text:
"Wells without water" and clouds "carried with a tempest" (hypo lailapos elaunomenai) both trade on the same disappointment — something that promises refreshment by its very appearance and delivers none, driven past by a storm rather than releasing the rain it seemed to carry.

"Great swelling words of vanity" is hyperonka mataiotētos, hyperonkos meaning "over-swollen, bombastic" — rhetoric inflated well past whatever substance actually supports it.

"Clean escaped" translates apopheugontas, an intensive compound — a full, decisive escape, not a partial or incomplete one, from those who had genuinely broken free of their former life before being drawn back in.

"Servants of corruption" (douloi tēs phthoras) closes the circle with 1:4's "corruption" (phthora) that believers were promised escape from — these teachers, promising liberty, are shown enslaved to the very thing salvation was meant to free anyone from.
translation: These are springs without water, and mists driven by a storm, for whom the gloom of darkness has been kept. For, speaking bombastic words of vanity, they entice, by the lusts of the flesh, by sensuality, those actually escaping from the ones living in error, promising them freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption; for by what a man is overcome, by this he has been enslaved.

label: 2 Peter 2:20–22
text:
"The latter end is worse with them than the beginning" restates, in blunt terms, a principle already implied throughout the chapter — a partial, temporary escape from corruption that is later abandoned leaves a person in a worse position than never having escaped at all.

"Better...not to have known" sets up a comparison of degree, not of moral neutrality — knowledge itself, once genuinely possessed and then turned from, becomes an aggravating factor rather than a merely wasted opportunity.

The two proverbs that close the chapter — the dog to its vomit (quoting Proverbs 26:11 almost exactly) and the washed sow to the mire — both describe an external cleansing that never reached the animal's actual nature; a dog stays a dog, and a scrubbed pig, given the chance, will always find the mud again.
translation: For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, having known it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. It has happened to them according to the true proverb: A dog, returning to its own vomit, and a sow, having washed, to wallowing in the mire.

label: 2 Peter 3:1–4
text:
"Stir up" is diegeirō, an intensive compound of "to wake" — a thorough, complete rousing, not a gentle nudge.

"Pure" translates eilikrinē, a rare and almost poetic word built from heilē, "the sun's heat," and krinō, "to judge" — literally, something judged and found sound by holding it up to sunlight, the ancient method for checking pottery or fabric for hidden flaws.

"Scoffers" is empaiktai, a rare word for professional mockers, and their walking "after their own lusts" is present tense, a continuous, habitual manner of life rather than an occasional lapse.

"Fell asleep" (ekoimēthēsan) is the standard early-Christian euphemism for death — the scoffers' argument trades precisely on this word's gentleness, treating the fathers' quiet deaths as proof that nothing dramatic will ever interrupt the world's routine.
translation: This is now, beloved, a second letter I am writing to you, in both of which I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder, to remember the words spoken beforehand by the holy prophets, and the commandment of your emissaries, the Lord and Savior, through us — knowing this first, that in the last days mockers will come with mocking, going according to their own lusts, and saying: Where is the promise of his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue thus from the beginning of creation.

label: 2 Peter 3:5–7
text:
"Willingly are ignorant" translates a striking construction — lanthanei, "it escapes notice," paired with thelontas, "being willing" — the ignorance is not innocent; it escapes them because they have chosen for it to.

"Overflowed" is kataklystheis, the direct root of the English "cataclysm" — the flood functions here as the archetype the very word for catastrophe still carries.

"Kept in store" is tethēsaurismenoi, built on thēsauros, "treasure" — the present heavens and earth are pictured as being deliberately stored up, treasured, held in reserve for a purpose not yet realized, exactly as the ancient world was once held in reserve for judgment by water.
translation: For, this escaping their notice by their own willing, that heavens existed long ago, and an earth held together out of water and through water by the word of God, through which the world at that time, being deluged with water, was destroyed. But the present heavens and earth, by the same word, have been stored up for fire, being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men.

label: 2 Peter 3:8–9
text:
"Longsuffering" is makrothymei, present tense — literally "long-tempered," built from makros, "long," and thymos, "passion" — patience pictured as a fuse of unusual length, actively burning slowly rather than merely present as a static trait.

"Not willing" uses boulomenos, the verb of deliberate, settled resolve, not the weaker word for a passing wish — God's reluctance toward anyone perishing is a fixed determination, not a soft preference.

"Come to" is chōrēsai, a spatial verb meaning "to make room for, to advance into" — repentance is pictured as a space to be entered and occupied, not merely an emotion to be felt.
translation: But let this one thing not escape you, beloved, that one day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slow concerning the promise, as some regard slowness, but is being longsuffering toward you, not wishing any to perish, but all to make room for repentance.

label: 2 Peter 3:10–13
text:
"Great noise" translates rhoizēdon, a rare, onomatopoeic adverb imitating a rushing, whistling sound — the noise an arrow makes cutting through the air, or a sudden gust of wind, packed into a single word.

"Elements" is stoicheia, the term for the basic building blocks of the physical order — whether the raw materials of matter itself or the heavenly bodies is debated, but either reading names something foundational, not incidental, being undone.

"Holy conversation and godliness" appears in the plural in the Greek — many specific holy ways of living and godly acts, not one abstract quality held in general.

"Hasting unto" is speudontas, present participle — actively, continuously speeding the day's coming forward, a striking claim that believers' own conduct is somehow bound up with the timing of what God has fixed.

"Wherein dwelleth righteousness" uses katoikei, "to dwell permanently, to settle down" — a deliberate contrast with the merely temporary "sojourning" language used throughout Peter's first letter; righteousness will not merely visit the new creation, it will make its home there.
translation: But the day of the Lord will come as a thief, in which the heavens will pass away with a rushing sound, and the elements, being burned with intense heat, will be dissolved, and the earth and the works in it will be found. Since all these things are being dissolved in this way, what sort of people ought you to be in holy ways of living and godly acts, awaiting and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens, being on fire, will be dissolved, and the elements, burning with intense heat, will melt? But according to his promise we are awaiting new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.

label: 2 Peter 3:14–16
text:
"Diligent" repeats spoudasate, the same root Peter reached for repeatedly across chapter 1 — the disciplined effort applied there to building virtue is applied here, at the letter's close, to being found ready.

"Without spot, and blameless" (aspiloi kai amōmētoi) reverses, almost word for word, the "spots and blemishes" used of the false teachers in 2:13 — the sacrificial vocabulary that condemned them is precisely what believers are urged to become.

Paul's letters are placed here alongside "the other scriptures" (tas loipas graphas) — a remarkably early testimony that Paul's own writings were already being received as Scripture in their own right, not merely as respected correspondence.

"Wrest" is strebousin, a verb originally used of torture on the rack — willful misinterpretation is pictured as a violent twisting of the text's own body, not an innocent misreading.

"Unstable" is astēriktoi, built on the same root as stērigmou, "stability," at the start of verse 17 — the letter's closing warning and its closing exhortation are tied together by a single word, negated in one place and affirmed in the other.
translation: Therefore, beloved, awaiting these things, be diligent to be found by him in peace, spotless and unblemished; and regard the longsuffering of our Lord as salvation, as also our beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you, as also in all his letters, speaking in them concerning these things, in which are some things hard to understand, which the untaught and unstable twist, as also the rest of the scriptures, to their own destruction.

label: 2 Peter 3:17–18
text:
"Led away with" is synapachthentes, a compound built on "carried along" with the prefix "together with" attached — being swept off in company with others already being swept away, not falling alone.

"Error" is planē, "a wandering, a deception" — the same family of words that gives the modern "planet," a body that appears to wander against the fixed stars.

"Stedfastness" is stērigmou, directly answering "unstable" (astēriktoi) from the previous verse — the very stability the false teachers' victims lack is exactly what Peter's readers are warned not to lose.

"Grow" is auxanete, present imperative — a continuous, ongoing growth commanded as an unbroken habit, the letter's final word of instruction before its closing doxology.
translation: You, then, beloved, knowing this beforehand, guard yourselves, so that you are not carried away together with the error of unprincipled men and fall from your own steadfastness. But keep growing in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory, both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.
